label: bm-mycelium-living-materials
topic: Mycelium and engineered living materials: could a living layer be the swelling layer of a humidity bilayer printed on Formlabs machines?
summary: Particulate mycelium composites (the usual product) are a poor swelling layer. They are stiff only to 0.03-4.44 MPa compressive, take up 6-436 % water, shrink 2.78-17 % on drying, swell 205-244 % through the thickness but under about 7 % in plane, vary a lot from specimen to specimen, and some batches fail (contamination, disintegration). The Buehler-corpus 'robust myco-composite' (Shen 2024) is a paste-printed (2 mm layers) chitosan/cellulose/coffee body colonised for 14 days; it reaches 160 MPa modulus and 0.72 MPa strength, but the mycelium weakens the substrate and acts as a hydrophobic skin (contact angle 117 to 138 degrees) and a weld. It is a skin or protective layer, not a large-swelling layer, and nobody has grown it on a Formlabs resin. Two living layers do have measured humidity strain in air and could be the active layer of a bilayer. (1) Nie 2026: a Trametes versicolor film made of two grown layers (0.22 and 0.30 mm), E = 23.7 MPa with PVA and glycerol, 374.9 mg/g moisture uptake at 85 % RH, volume expansion 9.27 % vs 3.38 % (30 to 85 % RH), bends in 8 min. (2) Wang 2017: dried microbial cells, 1 micrometre on 200 micrometre latex, volume linear in RH, fitted modulus 70 MPa, response in seconds, 100 cycles. My own calculation (linear Timoshenko, project-record f(m,n) with ceiling 3/2): both are far softer than Formlabs rigid resins, so they only work against a soft elastomer (Silicone 40A, Flexible 50A, Flexible 80A V2) where the optimum active/passive thickness ratio is 0.18-0.50 and f is 1.40-1.49. Against Rigid 10K the optimum needs a 20-fold thicker active layer and f falls to about 0.01. Predicted curvature is an upper bound: about 56 1/m linear, 13-15 1/m after the 3.8-4.4x derating the project record gives for soft films. Blockers: contamination, batch variability, no building-product standard or fire class, a living layer that must be added after printing (SLS sintering and SLA post-cure would kill it), plasticiser in the Nie film, 1-year dormancy limit, and no data on adhesion or growth on photopolymer resins.
lay_summary: Mushroom 'roots', called mycelium, can be grown into a leathery sheet, and some of those sheets curl when the air gets damp, like a pine cone. We looked for a living layer that could bend a printed strip when humidity changes. The usual mycelium building blocks, grown on sawdust, swell a lot but mainly in thickness and they are weak and inconsistent, so they are a poor choice. Two other options look better: a mushroom-root film grown in a dish, and a hair-thin coat of dried bacteria. Both swell a few percent in damp air, far more than the printing plastics do, and the bacteria coat reacts in seconds. They are soft, so they only bend a printed strip well if the strip is a rubbery printing resin, not a hard one. The big unknowns are keeping the living layer clean and consistent and getting it approved for buildings.

glossary.plain: The root-like thread network of a fungus, which can be grown into a solid material.
A material where mycelium grows through and glues together another material such as sawdust or a printed frame.
Two thin layers stuck together; if one swells more than the other, the strip curls.
A number up to 1.5 that says how well a two-layer strip turns a swelling difference into bending; the project proved the 1.5 limit.
Stiffness: how much force it takes to stretch or bend a material by a given amount.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water vapour the air can hold.
Swelling in the thin direction (making a board fatter) versus swelling along the surface (what makes a strip curl).
A fungal protein that coats surfaces and makes them repel water.
Letting mycelium grow onto a printed object from a bed of living mycelium instead of mixing it into the ink.
A film whose two faces are different, named after the two-faced Roman god.
'Generally recognised as safe': a US food-safety status for an organism.
Unwanted bacteria or moulds taking over the culture.
Two 3D-printing methods: curing liquid resin with light, or fusing plastic powder with a laser.
A scale for how hard a rubbery material feels; lower is softer.

findings.claim: Shen et al. (MIT, Buehler group) print a chitosan/cellulose/coffee-ground biocomposite and colonise it with mycelium by indirect inoculation; the colonised composite has Young's modulus 160 MPa and tensile strength 0.72 MPa, reported as the strongest mycelium composite to date.
findings.source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38315077 (published abstract, Mater. Horiz. 2024, 10.1039/d3mh01277h); body text from arXiv v2 https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12151 because the RSC page returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare) in this run
findings.evidence_quote: We found that our method yields the strongest mycelium composite reported to date with a modulus of 160 MPa and tensile strength of 0.72 MPa

findings.claim: In that paper mycelium colonisation WEAKENS the printed substrate (printed uncolonised composite is about 340 MPa stiffness and 4.2 MPa tensile strength), so the living phase is a skin and a welding agent, not a reinforcement.
findings.value: uncolonised printed ~340 MPa / 4.2 MPa vs colonised 160 MPa / 0.72 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: In comparison to the uncolonized biocomposite, growth of mycelium actually weakens the material.

findings.claim: Printed uncolonised composite: approximate stiffness 340 MPa and tensile strength 4.2 MPa.
findings.evidence_quote: At approximate stiffness of 340 MPa and tensile strength of 4.2 MPa for the printed composite

findings.claim: Typical mycelium composites, per Shen et al., have ultimate tensile strength up to 0.20 MPa and modulus up to 7.13 MPa, in the range of lightweight foams.
findings.evidence_quote: The upper limits of reported ultimate tensile strength and modulus of mycelium composites measure 0.20 MPa and 7.13 MPa respectively

findings.claim: Colonisation time on the printed substrate is typically 14 days (indirect inoculation on a bed of living mycelium); Ecovative substrate is pre-incubated 5 days.
findings.evidence_quote: until fully colonized as indicated by development of a full mycelium skin around the sample, typically a period of 14 days

findings.claim: The mycelium skin raises water contact angle from 117 to 138 degrees; the skin loses only 4.5 degrees in 30 s, which the authors attribute to hydrophobins.
findings.evidence_quote: resulted in the formation of a smooth “skin” with improved hydrophobicity as measured by an increase in water contact angle from 117º to 138º (Fig. 5a)

findings.claim: Colonised composite absorbs less water and swells less in volume than non-colonised composite over 24 h submersion, though it first swells quickly; the numbers are only in Fig. 5c and could not be read from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: the fully colonized composite exhibited lower water absorption and volume swelling than non-colonized samples after being submerged for 24 hours

findings.claim: Shen et al. printed with 2.5 mm extrusion width and 2 mm layer height, about 25 to 40 times coarser than Form 4 SLA layers (50-100 um), so the route is a paste printer, not a Formlabs printer.
findings.value: 2.5 mm width; 2 mm layer; 0.5 mm resolution
findings.evidence_quote: 2.5 mm extrusion width, 2 mm layer height, and 0.5 mm system resolution

findings.claim: Mycelium bridged gaps of up to 8 mm between printed biocomposite regions ('bio-welding'), used to make foldable containers and mycelium textiles.
findings.evidence_quote: In preliminary experiments, mycelium was found to be capable of bridging gaps up to 8 mm between regions of printed biocomposite.

findings.claim: A second Buehler paper (Machine Learning: Science and Technology 2024) used a knowledge graph of 1000 biological-materials papers to PROPOSE a hierarchical mycelium-based composite; it is a computational proposal with no measured properties in the abstract.
findings.evidence_quote: the algorithm proposed an innovative hierarchical mycelium-based composite based on integrating path sampling with principles extracted from

findings.claim: Mycelium-bound composites (particulate substrate) reach only 0.03 to 4.44 MPa compressive strength.
findings.evidence_quote: MBC compressive strength ranges from 0.03 to 4.44 MPa

findings.claim: Water uptake of mycelium-bound composites depends strongly on species and substrate: 6 % (Ganoderma lucidum on beech sawdust) to 436 % (T. versicolor on rapeseed straw).
findings.evidence_quote: T. versicolor absorbs 26.8% and 30.3% water in wheat straw and flax, respectively, but 436% in rapeseed straw.

findings.claim: Drying shrinkage of mycelium composites is reported between 2.78 % and 17 %, wood-like and wider than plastics (0.3-2.5 %).
findings.evidence_quote: which reported MBC shrinkages between 2.78% and 17%

findings.claim: Bamboo-sawdust composites shrank 3.14-5.83 % against 9.80-16.66 % for corn-pericarp composites across fungal species (2024 study quoted by the review).
findings.evidence_quote: MBCs made from bamboo sawdust had lower shrinkage (3.14% to 5.83%) than those made from corn pericarp (9.80% to 16.66%) across various fungal species

findings.claim: Elsacker 2019 (T. versicolor, hemp, 28 C, 8 + 8 days growth, oven-dried at 70 C) measured average shrinkage of 9 % (loose hemp) in its Table 2; the review quotes 15 % pine softwood, 10 % flax, 9 % hemp.
Contamination is a measured failure mode: flax-dust and straw-dust samples grew slowly and were systematically contaminated, so they were dropped from testing.
findings.evidence_quote: A slow growth and systematic contamination for all flax dust (FD) and straw dust (SD) samples was observed.

findings.claim: Typical incubation for moulded composites is about 10 days, starting at about 70 % water, then oven-drying to stop growth.
findings.evidence_quote: A 10-day incubation period allows mycelium facilitating substrate cohesion, forming a 3D network of fungal and plant fibres.

findings.claim: 2026 hemp-hurd mycelium composites (P. ostreatus, G. applanatum; 14 d in mould, hot-pressed 100 C) take up 309 to 356 % water in 2-72 h at 40 C (formulation 2) and swell through thickness by 205 to 244 %.
findings.evidence_quote: Formulation 2 exhibited the highest water uptake, increasing from 309 ± 49% after 2 h to a maximum mean value of 356 ± 28% after 72 h

findings.claim: Swelling is almost entirely through-thickness: width and length change stays below about 7 %, so in-plane (bilayer-relevant) swelling is far smaller than the headline numbers, and wet integrity is poor (some formulations fell apart).
findings.evidence_quote: In contrast, in-plane dimensional changes were limited, with width and length changes generally remaining below approximately 7%.

findings.claim: Best mean compressive stress 5.7 MPa; best flexural stress 4.6 MPa with flexural modulus 627 MPa, but with very large scatter (SD 285 MPa on the modulus).
findings.evidence_quote: The highest mean maximum compressive stress was 5.7 ± 1.2 MPa, whereas the highest mean maximum flexural stress and flexural modulus were 4.6 ± 2.1 MPa and 627 ± 285 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: One formulation (no. 5) disintegrated during handling and could not be tested, showing batch-level failure.
findings.evidence_quote: the resulting material exhibited insufficient macroscopic cohesion and disintegrated during handling, preventing reproducible specimen preparation.

findings.claim: Mycelium grown 21 days on 3D-printed wood-PLA gyroid scaffolds gives yield strength 7.29 MPa (50 % porosity) and thermal conductivity 0.012 W/mK (90 % porosity); colonisation raised yield strength by 50-78 % at 70-90 % porosity.
findings.evidence_quote: of 7.29 ± 0.65 MPa for 50% porosity MBC

findings.claim: In the gyroid work the printed scaffold is dip-coated in a nutrient (peptone-malt-agar) solution before inoculation and grown 21 days; 40 mm cubes at 70 % porosity were covered in 14 days.
findings.evidence_quote: The fungus is then inoculated and grown for 21 days.

findings.claim: Fomes fomentarius growth on FDM PLA and PLA/hemp bars has only a minor effect on PLA's tensile properties; autoclave pre-treatment can significantly weaken the printed material.
findings.evidence_quote: The results indicate that mycelial colonization has a minor impact on the mechanical properties of PLA

findings.claim: Luo et al. 2025 print a mycelium-inoculated paste ('Mycofluid', coffee grounds 54.9 wt %, brown-rice flour 13.7 %, water 24.7 %) and show living mycelium can fuse separate prints.
findings.evidence_quote: Notably, we demonstrate how living mycelium can fuse separate prints, enabling complex geometries that are otherwise challenging to 3D print as one part.

findings.claim: Dense pure-mycelium sheets from S. commune dikaryons reach tensile strength up to 47.29 MPa and Young's modulus 0.69-2.06 GPa (monokaryon: 4.62-7.77 MPa and 0.38-0.64 GPa), i.e. polymer-film territory.
findings.evidence_quote: The highest σ was recorded for S139 and P351, with 47.29 MPa and 47.16 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: Liquid-culture pure-mycelium materials from three species: tensile strength 4.5-6.3 MPa, elongation at break 0.8-1.6 %, Young's modulus 408-710 MPa; species matters little.
findings.evidence_quote: The Young’s modulus of the PMMs also showed relatively small differences ranging between 408 and 710 MPa.

findings.claim: Pure-mycelium fibrous materials from Ganoderma lucidum and Pleurotus ostreatus were all hydrophobic, with water contact angle above 120 degrees; grown on cellulose they are stiffer.
findings.evidence_quote: All the developed fibrous materials were hydrophobic with water contact angles higher than 120°.

findings.claim: Nie et al. 2026 (Nat. Commun.) grow Trametes versicolor mycelium membranes that are intrinsically two-layered (aerial layer A, nutrient-side layer B); plasticised with 10 % PVA + 10 % glycerol the optimised film has E = 23.7 MPa, elongation 36 %.
findings.evidence_quote: with proper E (23.7 MPa), enough EG (36%) and T (1.0 MJ·m −3 ) values

findings.claim: That mycelium film takes up 374.9 mg/g moisture at 25 C and 85 % RH (5 cycles), i.e. about 37 % of its dry mass, reversibly.
findings.evidence_quote: average moisture uptake of 374.9 mg·g −1 (25 °C, 85% RH) in 5 consecutive cycles

findings.claim: Micro-CT between 30 % and 85 % RH gives bulk (volumetric) moisture expansion 9.27 % for layer A and 3.38 % for layer B, a 2.7-fold contrast between the two grown layers.
findings.evidence_quote: Bulk moisture expansion rate ( ε b ) was higher for layer A (9.27%) than layer B (3.38%)

findings.claim: Layer thicknesses of the Janus film are 0.22 mm (A) and 0.30 mm (B), so the film is about 0.5 mm thick; a 5 x 25 mm strip bends within 8 min when RH goes from 20 % to 85 %.
findings.evidence_quote: For layer A and B, average thickness was measured as 0.22 and 0.30 mm, respectively.

findings.claim: Strips programmed by geometry and glycerol give bending angles from -19.0 to +43.2 degrees (reversible, RH-dependent).
findings.evidence_quote: a library of bending angles, (−19.0 ± 10.3)° to (43.2 ± 10.7)° was achieved

findings.claim: Dormant mycelium films are re-activatable but the dry storage period must be limited to within 1 year to keep spores alive; fresh membranes hold >90 % water and need a 20-day culture.
findings.evidence_quote: To maintain the livingness of spores in macerates, the dry storage period should be limited within 1 year.

findings.claim: The authors cite earlier work (Sinha et al., Adv. Mater. 2025) on humidity-responsive living S. commune films but say it lacked demonstrations and mechanism; Nie's own film was made with a plasticiser, so it is not pure mycelium.
findings.evidence_quote: The humidity-responsive behavior observed in living Schizophyllum commune films by Sinha et al. provides promising inspiration.

findings.claim: Wang et al. 2017 (Sci. Adv.) made true bilayers: a 1 um cell layer (E. coli, B. subtilis, yeast) on a 200 um latex sheet bends at 15 % RH and flattens at 95 % RH.
findings.value: cell layer 1 um on latex 200 um; 15 % -> 95 % RH
findings.evidence_quote: The top layer is composed of E. coli cells (1 μm thick), and the bottom layer is a latex sheet (200 μm thick). It bends at 15% RH (A) and becomes flat at 95% RH (B).

findings.claim: Cell-layer modulus fitted from the Stoney-type model is 70 MPa; single-cell volume is linear in RH (AFM), V/V_wet = 0.345 RH + 0.667 with V_wet taken at 95 % RH.
findings.evidence_quote: The fitted elastic modulus of the cell layer is 70 MPa

findings.claim: From that volume law the linear (1/3-power) strain of the cell layer is -10.3 % between 15 % and 95 % RH and -5.3 % between 30 % and 70 % RH (own calculation).
findings.source: own calculation: scripts/bm-mycelium-living-materials/bilayer_candidates.py (uses the formula quoted above)

findings.claim: Films respond within a few seconds and showed no change in bending after 100 dry-wet cycles (fabric samples).
findings.evidence_quote: biohybrid films that can reversibly change shape and biofluorescence intensity within a few seconds in response to environmental humidity gradients

findings.claim: The garment used B. subtilis (US FDA GRAS status); the E. coli shoe prototype was flagged as not GRAS, to be replaced by GRAS species before commercialisation.
findings.evidence_quote: The garment used B. subtilis , which has the status of GRAS given by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

findings.claim: Co-cultured mycelium + bacterial-cellulose films reach tensile strength 195.62 MPa and toughness 11.51 MJ/m3; haze is tuned from 16.0 to 78.5 % by culture duration (4-8 days).
findings.evidence_quote: the films achieve simultaneous high tensile strength (195.62 ± 9.06 MPa)

findings.claim: A Cordyceps militaris living fungal textile keeps metabolic activity, accepts yeast and Aspergillus co-cultures, and degrades almost completely in 41 days.
findings.evidence_quote: Environmental assessments confirm near-complete morphological degradation within 41 days.

findings.claim: Living building material (hydrogel + sand + bacteria): earlier prototype had no viable cells at 20 C and 24 % RH after about 80 % water loss, but adding 200 mM trehalose kept cells viable after 12 days at about 15 % RH, with 1-4 MPa compressive strength.
findings.value: no viable cells at 24 % RH (old); viable at ~15 % RH with trehalose; 1-4 MPa
findings.evidence_quote: Non-saturated (gel/sand = 0.13) and saturated (gel/sand ratio = 0.3) LBMs with 200 mM trehalose show viable cells after curing for 12 days under ambient conditions (22°C and RH of approximately 15%).

findings.claim: Mycelium is far less flammable than PLA or PMMA in micro-scale calorimetry (peak heat release 67 W/g vs 375 and 446 W/g; char 23 wt %), but this is a material test, not a building fire classification.
Variability and contamination are the stated reasons mycelium cannot yet reach industrial product certification.
findings.evidence_quote: The lack of consistency and reproducibility of a specific material profile, therefore, prevents the scaling up of mycelium in both size and quantity to reach an industry-standard level of product certification.

findings.claim: Fungal material production carries long cycles, contamination risk and multi-step processing like other fermentation industries.
findings.evidence_quote: These variables include long production cycles, the risk of contamination

findings.claim: Mycelium composites do not fit the European construction-product regulation and CE-marking route; the benchmark harmonised standard for an equivalent panel is EN 13986.
findings.evidence_quote: This misalignment poses challenges particularly in comparing MBCs with other construction materials whose performance and standard basic requirements are determined by the Construction‐products regulations (CPR)

findings.claim: Many studies omit the fungal species used, which prevents reproduction.
findings.evidence_quote: However, many studies fail to specify the fungal species used in composite production, thus hindering reproducibility due to the omission of mycelium network details

findings.claim: A 2026 opinion paper on living architecture names system stability, environmental variability, biosafety and regulatory constraints as the open challenges for engineered living materials in buildings.
findings.evidence_quote: it also introduces challenges related to system stability, environmental variability, biosafety, and regulatory constraints.

findings.claim: Numerical check of the project-record ceiling: over a 161 x 161 log grid of (m, n) the maximum of f is 1.5000 and it is reached where m^2 n = 1; f is also unchanged under (m, n) -> (1/m, 1/n), so it does not matter which layer is called 1.

findings.claim: Linear strain equivalents (isotropic assumption, eps = (1+dV/V)^(1/3) - 1): Nie film layer A 3.00 %, layer B 1.11 %, difference 1.88 % (30 -> 85 % RH); Wang cell layer -10.3 % (15 -> 95 % RH) and -5.3 % (30 -> 70 % RH). Nie report that isolated layers A and B did NOT differ significantly in planar expansion, so the isotropic split is an assumption, not a measurement.

findings.claim: A mycelium film of E = 23.7 MPa is too soft to pair with the stiff Formlabs resins: with Rigid 10K (E 10 GPa) the optimum (m^2 n = 1) needs the active layer 20.5 times thicker than the passive one, and a 0.2 mm film on 0.6 mm gives only f = 0.008 (curvature 0.31 1/m). With soft elastomers it is near the ceiling: optimum t_active/t_passive = 0.184 (Silicone 40A), 0.276 (Flexible 50A), 0.495 (Flexible 80A V2). Elastomer moduli are the secant estimates in the project record (0.8, 1.8, 5.8 MPa; none is published).
findings.source: own calculation, script D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents2/scripts/bm-mycelium-living-materials/bilayer_candidates.py (inputs: f(m,n) from project record; E and strains from the sourced findings above; elastomer E from D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents/spec-formlabs-materials.json)

findings.claim: Linear-theory curvature of a 0.2 mm Nie-type film (eps 3.0 %) on 0.6 mm Flexible 50A is 55.9 1/m (radius 17.9 mm), but the project record says Timoshenko over-predicts soft printed films by 3.8-4.4x, giving 12.7-14.7 1/m (radius 68-79 mm). Treat the linear number as an upper bound.

findings.claim: Thin dried-cell film (E 70 MPa, eps 5.3 % for 30 -> 70 % RH) on a 0.2 mm Flexible 50A layer: f = 0.66 at 1 um, 1.37 at 10 um, 1.50 at 30 um (ceiling 1.5 reached near 30 um), i.e. at least ~10 um of cells is needed before the layer uses the bilayer well; a single 1 um monolayer wastes about half the ceiling. Linear-theory radius 2.9 mm at 10 um (derate as above).

findings.claim: CONFIRMS spec-architecture-gaps.json: mycelium composites 0.03-4.44 MPa compressive and 6-436 % water uptake. I re-read the same 2025 review (PMC12387367) and both ranges are in its text.
findings.evidence_quote: MBC compressive strength ranges from 0.03 to 4.44 MPa

findings.claim: DEEPENS/PARTLY CONTRADICTS the summary line in spec-architecture-gaps.json 'Mycelium composites are insulation-grade only': true for loose-particulate moulded composites, but dense or hybrid forms are far stiffer: pure-mycelium sheets E 0.4-2.06 GPa and UTS up to 47 MPa, printed-scaffold hybrids 7.29 MPa yield, Shen 160 MPa modulus.
findings.evidence_quote: The highest σ was recorded for S139 and P351, with 47.29 MPa and 47.16 MPa, respectively.

findings.claim: DEEPENS spec-architecture-gaps.json 'the cells die when the material dries at room humidity' (living building materials): that was true of the first prototype (no viable cells at 24 % RH) but Qiu 2021 shows trehalose keeps cells viable after 12 days at about 15 % RH.
findings.evidence_quote: Non-saturated (gel/sand = 0.13) and saturated (gel/sand ratio = 0.3) LBMs with 200 mM trehalose show viable cells after curing for 12 days under ambient conditions (22°C and RH of approximately 15%).

findings.claim: DEEPENS spec-resin-chemistry.json and spec-formlabs-materials.json (stock resins swell under 1 % in 24 h and no humid-air coefficient exists): living layers supply the missing active partner in AIR, not immersion. A mycelium film gives 3 % linear-equivalent (my estimate) and a dried-cell layer 5-10 % linear over 30-95 % RH, well above the 0.2-0.9 % that the earlier agent estimated for stock resins, but BELOW the 3.5-74 % that it recorded for printed PEG-acrylate hydrogels. The living-layer advantage is speed (seconds for cells, 8 min for the 0.5 mm mycelium film vs 24 h for stock resin), not size.

findings.claim: NO paper was found (Europe PMC, several queries) that grows mycelium on a Formlabs or other SLA/DLP photopolymer resin; the printed-substrate precedents use PLA/wood filament (gyroid, Fomes) or a coffee/chitosan paste (Shen, Luo). Fungal growth on cured methacrylate resin, and adhesion of a living film to it, are therefore untested.
findings.source: Europe PMC queries listed in reproduce step 6

key_claims.claim: The only measured in-air humidity data for a mycelium layer of bilayer relevance is Nie et al. 2026: a T. versicolor film with two grown layers, E = 23.7 MPa, volumetric moisture expansion 9.27 % (layer A) vs 3.38 % (layer B) between 30 % and 85 % RH, 0.22-0.30 mm per layer. (It contains PVA and glycerol.)
key_claims.evidence_quote: Bulk moisture expansion rate ( ε b ) was higher for layer A (9.27%) than layer B (3.38%)

key_claims.claim: A micrometre-thin layer of dried microbial cells is the largest humidity-strain living layer with a fitted model: cell volume is linear in RH, 1 um of cells on 200 um latex bends at 15 % RH and flattens at 95 % RH, and the fitted cell-layer modulus is 70 MPa.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The top layer is composed of E. coli cells (1 μm thick), and the bottom layer is a latex sheet (200 μm thick). It bends at 15% RH (A) and becomes flat at 95% RH (B).

key_claims.claim: Particulate mycelium composites are a poor swelling layer: water uptake 6-436 %, drying shrinkage 2.78-17 %, and swelling is almost all through-thickness (205-244 %) with in-plane change under about 7 % and poor wet integrity.
key_claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, in-plane dimensional changes were limited, with width and length changes generally remaining below approximately 7%.

key_claims.claim: The Buehler-corpus myco-composite (Shen 2024) reaches 160 MPa modulus and 0.72 MPa tensile strength only on a coarse paste-printed substrate (2 mm layers) and the living phase weakens that substrate; no growth on a Formlabs resin has been published that I could find.
key_claims.evidence_quote: We found that our method yields the strongest mycelium composite reported to date with a modulus of 160 MPa and tensile strength of 0.72 MPa

recommendations: Do not use particulate mycelium-bound composite as the swelling layer: swelling is through-thickness, scatter is large (627 +/- 285 MPa flexural modulus), and wet integrity fails. Use mycelium, if at all, as a thin hydrophobic skin on the passive side.

If a living layer is wanted, make the PASSIVE layer a soft Formlabs elastomer (Silicone 40A, Flexible 50A or Flexible 80A V2), not Rigid 10K: with E_active about 24-70 MPa the optimum thickness ratio (m^2 n = 1) is only reached against a soft partner. Target active layer about 18-50 % of the passive thickness for a mycelium film, or at least 10-30 um of dried cells on 0.2 mm elastomer.

First experiment (cheap, reproducible): a dried B. subtilis or yeast cell layer sprayed on a 0.2 mm printed Flexible 50A strip, cycled 30 to 70 % RH in a salt-solution chamber; measure curvature and compare with the derated prediction (derate the linear-theory number by 3.8-4.4x). Second: a Nie-type Trametes film (needs a mycology lab) laminated to Silicone 40A.
Add the living layer AFTER printing and post-cure; do not put it through SLS sintering or SLA UV post-cure. Test fungal growth and adhesion on cured resin coupons first, since no literature exists.

For the architecture pitch, present the living layer as a research option with a non-living, certifiable fall-back (the elastomer bilayer, or dried-cell or killed-mycelium film) because no standard, fire class or CE route exists for mycelium products.
